entries.title: Democrats Are Launching a New Way to Coordinate With Outside Groups
entries.summary: A new agreement between Swing Left and official Democratic infrastructure could be a template for future data-sharing and coordination.
entries.content:
The Democratic National Committee and a liberal organizing group have struck a first-of-its-kind deal among Democrats to seamlessly share voter data collected on the campaign trail, bolstering coordination between outside organizations, party committees and individual campaigns.

The agreement was reached between Swing Left, the Democratic Data Exchange (the Democratic entity that houses the party's voter data), the DNC and the Association of State Democratic Committees. It is in part an effort to retrofit how the party conducts its field programs up and down the ballot. The goal is to allow Democrats to effectively pool their resources to most effectively and efficiently engage voters.

Officials say they hope the agreement becomes a template for deals between other outside groups and the official Democratic Party infrastructure.

“The DNC is committed to organizing year-round, ensuring Democrats up and down the ballot have the infrastructure to win in 2026, 2028, and beyond,” Catherine Tarsney Kahle, the DNC’s chief technology officer, said in a statement. “We are proud to partner with Democratic Data Exchange and Swing Left to put critical, ground-level voter data directly into the hands of campaigns nationwide and look forward to continuing that work with others.”

Outside groups that ran door-to-door voter outreach efforts were for years legally prohibited from coordinating with candidates and the party infrastructure; they were able to share only a subset of the data they collected from voters, which officials say was of limited use. But a 2024 advisory opinion from the Federal Election Commission allowed the two sides to collaborate with their field programs.

This deal takes the newly allowed coordination to the next level, allowing all parts of the wider Democratic ecosystem to share the entirety of the data they collect from each individual interaction with voters, and to do so instantly.

“That's what this agreement does,” said Yasmin Radjy, executive director of Swing Left. “It allows every volunteer conversation to strengthen campaigns, state parties and organizations across the country. It will help Democrats compete in 2026 while ensuring we're not starting from scratch again in 2028.”

Swing Left has launched a revamped effort this election cycle to reach independent and Republican-leaning voters, hoping its new field program can help Democrats win congressional majorities in purple districts and states.

Some Democratic officials believe the party has fallen behind Republican-backed field programs in recent elections, especially after Donald Trump's 2024 campaign successfully identified and persuaded many voters who don’t often turn out to vote. They hope the Democratic Party, boosted by agreements like these, can catch up in this year’s midterm elections.

entries.title: Normies’ Left Turn
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Why some normie Democrats are backing El-Sayed. Wisconsin’s gubernatorial race gives DSA its biggest test yet. Moreno says his ex-son-in-law congressman is unfit for office. The DNC strikes a first-of-its-kind info-sharing deal. Why some candidates can’t say no to corporate cash. Democratic senators reject DSA’s push to axe the Senate. And: Trump’s plan to supercharge local immigration enforcement. 

THE LATEST

What’s happening in Michigan? The defining Democratic primary of the cycle — the Senate race between Rep. Haley Stevens and former Wayne County health department chief Abdul El-Sayed — is not only about how the left learned how to win, NOTUS’ Alex Roarty reports. It’s just as much about how badly the mainstream Democratic Party has lost trust.

Alex examines the average, normie Democrats — Boomers, relatively affluent, Clinton-supporting types — who are on the El-Sayed train. Many of them voted against El-Sayed in 2018, when he ran for governor as the left’s alternative to Democrat Gretchen Whitmer. He notched only 30% of the primary vote. But polls are showing him comfortably ahead in Tuesday’s Senate primary.

Progressive activists say privately that they think these voters’ movement toward candidates like El-Sayed is less about a newfound acceptance of lefty policies like single-payer health care, and more about anger with the Democratic establishment, Alex writes. Many Democrats once skeptical of Stevens now think she might have turned the corner in using attacks against her as slights against the whole state — but the election may hinge on whether normies take a ride with the left’s loftier ideas instead of the establishment’s status quo.

The big example, of course, is the debate around Israel. NOTUS’ Akbar Shahid Ahmed connects the dots, tracing how the debate has become a simple way for many Democrats to find the outsider fighter they’re looking for. “Palestine is a credibility test now,” said Greg Krieg of the American Priorities PAC, which was built to counter AIPAC. “If voters think you won’t be honest about it, they won’t trust you on anything else.”

The Michigan primary could be summarized in one sentence: El-Sayed is unabashedly pro-Palestine, Stevens is benefiting from millions in AIPAC spending, and that’s all many primary voters need to know.

Open tabs: Gulf States Pressed Trump to Hold Off on Iran Strikes and Pursue Talks (WSJ); For sale: early access to Trump's Truth Social posts (NPR); Republican Sen. Kennedy says he ‘wouldn’t bet my house’ on Blanche being confirmed (The Hill); RFK Jr. targets Fauci and pushes medical misinformation in fiery CNN interview (CNN); Former Texas Congresswoman, Fort Worth's first female mayor, Kay Granger dies (CBS)

From the campaign trail

Democratic socialists are facing their biggest test yet in Wisconsin’s chaotic primary for governor. It’s easier for Zohran Mamdani’s wing of the Democratic Party to find its footing in deeper blue states like New York, but Francesca Hong’s candidacy gives Dems the chance to assess a DSA-aligned candidate in a battleground state. Some voters have a “real fear” that Hong’s connections to the DSA won’t fare well in a state Trump carried in 2024, NOTUS’ Elena Schneider reports.

“In a super, super purple state, I’m worried she’s not going to catch the people on the fence,” said one attendee at a Hong campaign event in Franklin, Wisconsin.

But Hong sees the rise of the DSA brand as a way to bridge gaps in the party’s voting base, saying it’s successful “especially among the voters who are hardest to reach, which are Gen Z and millennials.”

The road to reelection is getting rockier for Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) after his ex-father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), said Miller should seek professional psychological help and “should not serve in the House,” citing allegations of domestic abuse against his daughter and granddaughter, NOTUS’ Jenna Monnin and Reese Gorman report. That came after Miller livestreamed a 20-minute denial of the accusations yesterday, vowed to keep running for reelection and posted files, videos and audio recordings to Dropbox.

But the numbers already weren’t looking good for Miller. His Democratic opponent in Ohio’s 7th Congressional District, Brian Poindexter, is polling at 44% to Miller’s 39% with 16% undecided, according to a recent poll conducted by a Republican firm and reviewed by NOTUS. That’s in a district Trump won by 11 percentage points in 2024.

Sharing is caring, or at least that's the message the Democratic National Committee hopes other outside groups take from its first-of-its-kind deal with the liberal organizing group Swing Left to seamlessly share voter data collected on the campaign trail. The DNC is hopeful that the deal can serve as a template for future collaboration after the FEC opened the door to sharing with outside groups.

“It will help Democrats compete in 2026 while ensuring we're not starting from scratch again in 2028,” Yasmin Radjy, executive director of Swing Left, told NOTUS’ Alex Roarty.

The life of the corporate donation taker. It’s chic in Democratic politics to say no to business-linked political action committees, but NOTUS’ Oriana González and Kadia Goba find it doesn’t protect members from the intense pressure to raise big sums — all the time. “I am deciding whether I'm going to committee or a meeting based on whether I have to meet with individual donors,” said one Democratic lawmaker caught in the middle. “That's fucked up.” Democrats without major name recognition or national donor networks say taking corporate contributions can save them literally hours of call time per week. That plus eagerness to help battleground races pushes some former corporate-donation rejecters into sighing heavily and taking the money.

From the Hill

The Senate prefers not to be abolished, thank you. “No,” Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) said flatly when NOTUS asked about the plank in the new Democratic Socialists of America platform calling for the Senate to be eliminated in favor of a unicameral legislature. Our Igor Bobic reports zero takers to the idea among senators who caucus with the Democrats.

NEW ON NOTUS

The Trump administration plans to supercharge immigration enforcement with $1.6 billion in grants to state and local police agencies through September 2027, NOTUS’ Jackie Llanos reports. The push far exceeds previous federal funding for the 287(g) program, which allows for coordination between federal and state entities on enforcement efforts. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin recently called the program “the greatest partnership we can have.”

entries.title: Wisconsin Is DSA’s Biggest Test Yet
entries.summary: Democratic socialist Francesca Hong has risen to the top of a chaotic gubernatorial primary, with major ramifications for Democrats’ future.
entries.content:
FRANKLIN, Wis. — The first, second and third questions for Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong at her meet-and-greet Thursday night revolved around her affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America.

Voters described a “real fear” she can’t win a general election for governor, questioned whether she’d tailor her policy platform to reach swing voters and asked for a primer on “what we can say to others when that concern comes up.”

This standing-room-only event captured Hong’s appeal — a packed, generationally diverse crowd, surrounded by dozens of hand-drawn signs for the once little-known state legislator — but it also reflected the angst of voters here. At times, it bordered on group therapy, with voters airing their concerns over Hong’s ability to win the governor’s race in a closely divided state that President Donald Trump won two years ago.

“In a super, super purple state, I’m worried she’s not going to catch the people on the fence,” said Faith Casselman, a 32-year-old medical education coordinator who attended the event.

This anxiety has defined much of the primary itself, as Hong’s opponents insist the state assemblymember would be unable to beat Rep. Tom Tiffany, the likely GOP nominee. As DSA candidates rack up victories in blue cities and districts, tapping into a deep discontent within the Democratic Party, Hong’s candidacy is the first test of it in a battleground state. The results, say Democrats in Wisconsin and Washington, will offer clues for how the party’s electorate might assess a potential DSA-aligned candidate, like New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, in the 2028 presidential primary.

“The Democratic brand is struggling. The Republican brand is struggling,” Hong told NOTUS in an interview. “The democratic socialist brand is starting to rise, especially among the voters who are hardest to reach, which are Gen Z and millennials.”

That isn’t a satisfactory answer, though, for some Wisconsin Democrats.

“If you’re trying to explain what DSA is or isn’t, you’re losing,” said a Wisconsin Democratic consultant not working with any of the gubernatorial candidates, who was granted anonymity to discuss the issue candidly.

Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, one of Hong’s opponents in the Aug. 11 primary, is left trying to make the argument that Wisconsin is not like the heavily Democratic places where the DSA has flourished this year. “New York City and the state of Wisconsin” are “different,” he told a dozen voters in the town of Baraboo, many of whom nodded along.

But as has been true in other major races this year, from Colorado to Maine to New Jersey, the Democratic establishment has struggled to fend off the rising far left. Wisconsin has turned into the most vivid showdown of those competing wings. Democrats in the state have seen a cast of traditional candidates rise and fall over the past month — all while that wing of the party has failed to coalesce around a single alternative.

In early July, Crowley dropped out and endorsed Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, when it appeared she was uniting moderate support. But Rodriguez dropped out just over a week later, after her campaign acknowledged widespread campaign finance irregularities. Crowley opted to get back into the race with an endorsement from Gov. Tony Evers, who had previously said he’d remain neutral; backers of another candidate, former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, decried the move as fracturing the center-left bloc again.

But then Thursday, Barnes, who’d been polling second-highest behind Hong, dropped out. In a video, he said the “front-runner is clear,” but the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel soon after published a story about concerns within the party that Barnes had allegedly used his political role to facilitate sexual relationships.

Crowley, along with state Sen. Kelda Roys and former Evers administration official Joel Brennan, were all polling in single-digits, while Hong hit 38 percent support in a Marquette University survey conducted in late July. About a third of voters were still undecided.

“It’s a collapse of the establishment combined with the bumbling of a bad situation,” said Steve Schale, a national Democratic consultant. “The socialist doesn't have to get to 50 percent to win. It requires the normie class — mainstream, establishment, whatever it is — failing to recognize that threat and rally around one person.”

In Wisconsin, several voters described the primary campaign as “chaotic” and “unsettling,” or “basically a reality show,” as Caitlin Hapsel, a 38-year-old Greendale resident at Hong’s event in Franklin, put it. Nyaga Kariuki, a 25-year-old Milwaukee voter, said “the moderates just did not get themselves together.”

Moderates’ disarray is worrying Eleanor Chiquoine, a 72-year-old voter from Sauk County who was happy to learn at Crowley’s event in Baraboo that Barnes had dropped out — “Oh, that’s good,” she said. She worries that Hong is “unelectable” but she hasn’t been able to settle on another option.

“Whether it is fair or not, being labeled, in this state especially, as a democratic socialist, then that might be a harder sell than you think, and that’s my concern,” Chiquoine said. She left with a Crowley yard sign, but she said she planned to keep it in her dining room until she finally picks a candidate.

Those are the kinds of voters Crowley needs to win over in less than two weeks, a tall order for a candidate who’s still trying to build his name recognition outside Milwaukee and with early voting already underway.

Crowley, in an interview with NOTUS, said he sees a “clear path to consolidate these undecided voters” that’s “based off of my experience” leading Milwaukee County and as a state legislator.

He’s now making an all-out sprint to introduce himself to voters, helped by a surge in fundraising since he jumped back into the race. Another Wisconsin Democratic operative, granted anonymity to speak candidly and not affiliated with a gubernatorial candidate, argued that 60 percent of the electorate “doesn’t want to vote for Fran,” giving Hong a “hard floor and low ceiling” of support.

“There are enough voters out there, and if Crowley can muster enough resources and reach them, he can really do something here,” the operative said. “But that’s a narrow path.”

Republicans, Crowley said, have picked Hong as their preferred candidate, pointing to the $3 million in TV ad spending the Republican Governors Association has dropped boosting her. In a post on X last week, Tiffany previewed his own line of attack on Hong, describing her as “a card-carrying socialist committed to abolishing the police, the Senate, and prisons.”

“That should make us pause a little bit, right?” Crowley said at his meet-and-greet in Baraboo. “If they have an opportunity to pick our nominees and say, ‘Oh, this is what communism looked like, or this is what socialism looks like,’ what does that do [to] defining who we are?”

Hong, a single mother and restaurant worker, has already started to define herself with voters, particularly younger, more liberal ones. Like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Hong has tapped into a potent organizing network, activating 7,000 volunteers and campaigning aggressively online. In answer to the voters who wanted to know how she’d combat labels of communism, Hong said her campaign has put out “clarification videos on our positions” and urged voters to zero in on Tiffany’s record.

“Bringing it back to policy is how we combat that word that, you know, they called Joe Biden and Tony Evers,” she said. “We don't even have a $10 minimum wage in our state, let alone $19, so what makes you think we're going to make socialism happen?”

Eddie Phanichkul, a Democrat who is running to flip a state Assembly district in suburban Milwaukee and attended Hong’s event in Franklin, acknowledged that “the socialism and the communism part is going to be a challenge.” But he said he believed they could “overcome that challenge because we just have to talk to people.”

In an interview with NOTUS after speaking to a few dozen voters at a community garden in Milwaukee, Hong said, “Wisconsin is ready for a democratic socialist governor because we're fighting for the things that people are asking for” and “a growing number of voters who feel left behind and unheard.”

“Electability is the person who wins the most votes,” she said when pressed on how she’d appeal to voters come November. “I’m a proud democratic socialist. I’m not advancing a brand. I'm focusing on the policies, the socialist policies that improve lives.”

But some Wisconsin Democrats, particularly those focused on down-ballot state legislative races, don’t buy that argument. Some privately fret that Hong’s candidacy, and her DSA labeling, could make flipping state legislative seats more difficult and that money from Democratic donors would dry up.

In the districts where there are “data center fights, she might turn into a folk hero, and other places, it may be more complicated,” said a third Wisconsin strategist who is not involved in the gubernatorial primary. “People are incandescent about prices, the Iran war and data centers, so the question is, is all of that enough to overcome the kinds of attack ads Tiffany will surely be running the day after the primary.”

It’s Hong’s positions on the “defund police” movement that gives those Wisconsin Democrats the most heartburn, they said. “She’s somewhat backed off of that, but the receipts are there, the tweets are there,” the first Democratic consultant said.

In 2020, Hong posted several times in support of defunding the police after the police shooting of Jacob Blake, a Black man, in Kenosha, Wisconsin. When a voter at the community garden event asked about her posts, Hong said, “We're in a different political climate than where we were five years ago, where the fearmongering of ‘defund’ is not as much of a priority when we're able to shift to the issues.”

Pressed on her position in the interview, Hong said her “values are established.”

“How I believe I can make sure that we have laws that reflect those values, that may evolve, but again, I think it's more important about what I'm going to do, and I'm going to be investing in things that we know would prevent crime,” she said. “I won't defund the police, and I cannot.”

DSA supporters, who gathered for their national meeting in Chicago over the weekend, are keeping a close eye on Wisconsin. Pennsylvania state Rep. Chris Rabb, a DSA-backed candidate who won his own multicandidate congressional primary this year, said that “if Hong wins, it will affirm that the platforms of democratic socialist candidates are more broadly embraced by a diverse electorate than corporate media and institutionalists within our electoral duopoly care to admit.”

The DSA does have some political history on its side. At the Franklin Public Library event, one voter brought up Wisconsin’s legacy as the first state to elect a socialist to Congress, in 1910.

“Don't apologize for being a democratic socialist,” the voter told Hong, rushing to shake her hand. “That's part of Wisconsin's tradition. Welcome.”

entries.title: Let’s Talk About the Massive Parking Garage Trump Wants to Build at Dulles
entries.summary: The 32,000-spot deck would surpass both existing parking capacity and what airport officials have said is needed.
entries.content:
It won’t exactly be the eighth wonder of the world, but it will be big — like, Guinness World Records big.

That’s what President Donald Trump promised last week when he unveiled plans to build a parking garage with space for 32,000 cars as part of his sweeping $22.5 billion renovation of Dulles International Airport.

“We’re building a massive … parking garage that will be right next to the terminal,” he said as he sat in front of a model of the new airport splayed across the top of the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. “It’ll be the largest garage in the world. Thirty-two thousand is big. It will be beautiful.”

The new parking deck got less attention than Trump’s announcement that the long-maligned mobile lounges that have shuttled passengers around Dulles since it opened in 1962 will be retired. But the detail does speak to many travelers’ annoyances with parking at Dulles, most of which is in satellite lots that require a shuttle to get to and from the main terminal.

Still, the big, beautiful deck-to-be stands as one of the Dulles renovation’s most surprising elements, since it would increase the airport’s parking capacity beyond what existing plans say is necessary, would add significant construction and airport operation challenges and would likely tower over the iconic terminal designed by Finnish architect Eero Saarinen.

Dulles currently has just over 22,000 parking spots for travelers, half of them in the distant economy lots. (This reporter almost lost track of their car in one of those lots.) While parking capacity fluctuates during the year (and can be viewed on a daily basis here), the Dulles Master Plan finalized by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority in July 2025 predicted that the existing number of parking spots available at the airport would suffice until at least 2045.

The plan noted that parking demand can fluctuate based on a number of factors, including “rises in gasoline prices could result in the reduced use of private vehicles.” (Gas prices have risen in the U.S. due in part to the ongoing conflict in Iran.) Still, the authority has already started planning to increase capacity to more than 28,600 spots, most of which would come through the construction of a new parking deck in front of the main terminal building where a surface lot now exists. That three-story deck — to be built between 2031 and 2034 — would fit 6,400 cars.

During his presentation, Trump seemed to be unaware of those plans. “We have an empty site right directly across the street that nobody wanted to tinker with, which is crazy,” he said.

His proposed parking deck — which would go in that same location — would accommodate five times as many cars. But few details exist: The deck wasn’t included in any of the renderings of the new airport that were put out by MWAA and the U.S. Department of Transportation (in fact, the main rendering kept the existing surface lot), and neither agency responded to specific questions about it from NOTUS.

The proposal has drawn skeptical reactions from some parking experts, including Bill Boyle, who owns a parking company in D.C. and runs the Washington Parking Association, a trade group.

“I looked up the biggest terminal garages in the U.S.,” he told NOTUS. “One is in Seattle and has 13,000 spots, and the other is in Detroit and has 11,500. This would be two-and-half times bigger than those two. That creates all kinds of issues with throughput of vehicles, wayfinding, ventilation and fire safety. There’s no precedent for building a parking deck this big.”

The world’s biggest parking lot is outside the West Edmonston Mall in Canada; it fits 20,000 cars in surface lots.

Without specifics, it’s impossible to know the actual physical scale of the proposed parking deck. But if MWAA kept to Trump’s pledge that most of it would be above-ground — “People don’t like down underneath,” he said — it could reach up to 15 stories. That would make the parking deck taller than the main terminal, which tops out at 65 feet.

It would also likely block most views of the historic terminal itself for passengers arriving by Metro or car, a concern that MWAA was already aware of with its plan for a three-story parking deck in front of the terminal. The master plan says it would address viewshed concerns by raising Saarinen Circle — a traffic circle in front of the terminal — “approximately 11 to 15 feet” above where it is now.

Boyle also said that building a record-breaking parking deck while the airport remains in operation would be challenging. “When you build it you’ll have to have cranes, materials and hauling routes,” he said. “You’re building an enormous garage in a constrained space and doing it while everything is functioning around it, and I don’t see anyone addressing that problem.”

It’s also unclear what such a parking deck would cost. A February 2026 report from the UCLA Institute of Transportation Studies estimated that each above-ground spot in a parking deck in and around Washington, D.C. can cost $29,000 to build. While that’s below the national average of $52,000, it would also mean that Trump’s proposed 32,000 parking spots could cost more than $900 million. (And that price tag would go up if any levels were underground; the UCLA report says that underground spots can cost $40,000 a piece to construct.)

Since November 2022, there has been an alternative for getting to and from Dulles: Metro. The Silver Line station Dulles sees anywhere from 1,300 to 4,300 entries per day, depending on the time of year.

“Why should we build the world's largest parking garage in the world on an airport we just invested $6B to connect to Metro?” tweeted Virginia Democratic Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell. 

But Trump has touted the proximity and convenience of his new parking deck. “People will literally be able to park their car and walk 15 yards and be in the terminal,” he said.

“It will be a parking garage the likes of which no one has even seen before!” offered one commenter on Reddit, in what could be seen as either a high compliment or a sarcastic criticism.

entries.title: Israel Is Defining Michigan's Primaries. Progressives Say That's Why They're Winning.
entries.summary: The debate among state Democrats is proving to be a microcosm of the discussion happening nationally within the party.
entries.content:
Rep. Haley Stevens recently lobbed a stunning accusation at her rival in the race to be Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed. “Everyone in America understands you want to blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans,” Stevens wrote Thursday on X.

Stevens is not Jewish. But she has received nearly $30 million — a record amount — in support from forces that have long dominated American discussion of Israel, the self-proclaimed Jewish state: the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and affiliated groups. El-Sayed, who could become the country’s first Muslim senator, has both condemned Israel and said he supports “equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike.”

Asked about her comments by a reporter on Saturday, Stevens responded: “There’s been a lot of talk from my opponent throughout this race about AIPAC, about foreign policy,” and mentioned El-Sayed campaigning with the streamer Hasan Piker, saying Piker “has been very antisemitic.” Piker has previously rejected similar characterizations of his views. Stevens’ campaign did not respond to an inquiry from NOTUS about her comments regarding El-Sayed.

Earlier in the week, Donavan McKinney, who is making a primary challenge against Rep. Shri Thanedar in Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, told NOTUS that as he campaigns, voters have demanded a “redistribution of resources” with clear implications for the U.S.-Israel relationship. As people speak of working three jobs or rent swallowing most of their Social Security checks, he sees their dire straits as inseparable from Washington choosing to fund Israel’s ongoing attacks on Palestinians and collaborating with Tel Aviv on “a war for no reason with Iran [that costs] $1 billion per day.”

Israel is inescapable in the dynamics around Michigan’s Tuesday primaries, making the elections there a microcosm of the larger debate within the Democratic Party over U.S. support for the country. An overwhelming majority of Democratic voters think the U.S. is too supportive of Israel, according to a late-June Quinnipiac poll. And the views of the American public writ large on the issue have trended downward in recent years — with a drastic split emerging between the preferences of the Democratic base and party leadership as the last Democratic president, Joe Biden, fueled Tel Aviv’s punishing offensives in Gaza and Lebanon.

Nationally, candidates and activists urging drastic changes to the U.S.’s Israel policy are now deeply enmeshed with those demanding an overall change to the Democratic Party’s positions and style, saying it has been soft on both Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Donald Trump. The establishment is pushing back: Gretchen Whitmer, Michigan’s Democratic governor, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer have endorsed Stevens against El-Sayed, and chief House Democrat Rep. Hakeem Jeffries backs Thanedar against McKinney. Schumer and Jeffries are firm Israel supporters. Will Lawrence, another insurgent House candidate tied to the party’s left flank, is battling two establishment-friendly rivals in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District.

Yet while political convention once recommended deference to hardline Israel allies, the situation in Michigan suggests rising forces in the Democratic Party are cementing a different strategy: being loud and proud in questioning Washington’s entanglement with Tel Aviv.

The 2026 midterms follow the 2024 cycle, in which American support for Israel first became a dominant national concern among Democrats. Like the current slate of progressive candidates, including El-Sayed and McKinney, those questioning Israel then faced intense pushback presenting them as needlessly divisive, and defenders of the U.S.-Israeli status quo still cite that election. The argument — pushed by voices like Rep. Dan Goldman (D-New York), a staunch Israel backer unseated in a primary this summer — is that the Uncommitted campaign, which began in Michigan and urged Democrats in several states to reject Biden in their primaries votes to send an electoral message to shift his Gaza policy, hurt the party. Goldman argued on X that Uncommitted “was significantly responsible for Trump 2.0.” Abbas Alawieh, an Uncommitted co-founder, is now running for state senate in Michigan with the backing of many of the organizations supporting fellow progressives. Alawieh has said he voted for Kamala Harris, and Uncommitted’s defenders say its goal was to warn Democrats about a vulnerability so they could win.

Today, Israel skeptics say the success of their movements in Democratic primaries in Colorado and New York earlier this summer has already demonstrated the growing popularity of changing the American relationship with Israel. Rather than treat Michigan as definitive, they hope it will entrench a trend — and be influenced by momentum elsewhere.

“This is a national movement too,” McKinney said, recalling his trip to Denver in June to campaign for Melat Kiros, a fellow challenger to a Democratic incumbent who entered national politics because of the Gaza war. “To see the energy on the ground — We were like, ‘I hope it spreads.’”

He continued: “People around the country are just tired of status quo politicians.”

Kiros and fellow progressives, including two others who won primaries this cycle, have stumped for candidates in Michigan during the primary races’ final weeks, and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), a progressive leader, visited the state to campaign for McKinney and El-Sayed last month. Locally, their coalition includes figures like Eboni Taylor, who’s running for state senate and whom Sanders has endorsed. Ed Rushton, an adviser to Taylor, cast the fight against AIPAC as similar to a deeply local issue: He said its operations resemble those of Detroit-based energy company DTE, in focusing on silencing critique from politicians from both parties — rather than supporting a positive agenda — and pumping excessive money into races. Stevens’ opponents argue, for instance, that there is no guarantee AIPAC and its partners will continue supporting her through November should they succeed in quashing El-Sayed.

The alliance among progressives means they can vouch for each other to those who might be skeptical of one, Rushton noted — including those wary of growing discussion of Israel in politics, and those highlighting the issue.

Some voters and even elected Democrats in Michigan have expressed concern about the political influence of Arab Americans, the community to which El-Sayed and Uncommitted’s leaders belong. At a recent campaign stop at a senior-living center, Rushton said, a person said they did not want “these Arabs to run the show,” an apparent criticism of Taylor’s endorsement from Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D), the sole Palestinian American in Congress.

“I almost appreciated them saying that” for the chance to respond, Rushton said, to what he calls “an attempt to remarginalize Arab Americans disguised as a reclaiming of the Democratic Party” after the loss to Trump.

“Across the state, 70,000 white women voted for Whitmer twice and voted for Trump in 2024. Yet somehow this is an Arab issue?” Rushton told NOTUS. He said Taylor responds to similar comments while canvassing by describing her personal trust in Tlaib, El-Sayed and Alawieh. Stevens has falsely claimed El-Sayed led Uncommitted and rejected Harris in 2024.

Usamah Andrabi, the communications director for the progressive group Justice Democrats, said the Michigan progressives can jointly “build power for the working class in working class communities” while using the 2024 experience to their own benefit, to argue that mainstream Democrats enabled the rise of a Republican trifecta federally.

“The establishment has spent so many years trying to convince everyday people they cannot challenge the billionaire class … [now] it is up to the establishment whether they want to use the campaigns we’re building as a roadmap,” he said. Justice Democrats formally endorsed McKinney and is, per Andrabi, “supportive from afar” of El-Sayed and Lawrence.

Part of that blueprint is a clear position on Israel. Greg Krieg of the American Priorities PAC, which explicitly aims to counter AIPAC spending, told NOTUS: “Palestine is a credibility test now. If voters think you won’t be honest about it, they won’t trust you on anything else.”

American Priorities has spent more than $650,000 in Michigan, he said.

Progressives say a central part of their strength is the excitement that drives grassroots ground organizing. In Michigan, they have the benefit of several aligned campaigns running simultaneously, “working to change the face of Congress for something much bigger” in terms of a policy shift, said Beth Miller, the political director of the organization Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP) Action.

Her group’s endorsement of El-Sayed was its first Senate endorsement and itself an indicator of the Democratic evolution on Israel: JVP is explicitly anti-Zionist. Miller traced the development to years of work by organizers focused on what she called American “complicity in Israeli apartheid and ethnic cleansing” that has grown significantly since the Gaza war began in October 2023.

El-Sayed was long on the group’s radar, she said, “not coming in trying to ride the coattails.”

Alongside his message, JVP emphasizes “the truth there is no ‘Jewish’ opinion on Israel or Palestine – as long as there has been Zionism, there have been anti-Zionist Jews,” Miller said.

Amid the optimism among progressives, they still have determined detractors in Michigan — including among Democratic voters and persuadable Trump voters, groups from which their candidates will need support in November. The handling of Israel is a particular focus for those who remain leery, though seemingly more over its impact on domestic politics than policy choices abroad: Stevens supporters argue El-Sayed and allies focused on pushing the party over Gaza created unnecessary and even dangerous negativity at a party convention in April. On Thursday, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, who is Jewish, said she will not attend the state party’s August convention over fears for her safety. Nessel’s critics say their opposition to her is over her attempted prosecutions of anti-war protesters at the University of Michigan.

Some Democrats maintain that the party and voters it needs won’t coalesce around progressive candidates in the general election, and those divisions could aid the GOP, with some hinting they might never back El-Sayed if he triumphs over Stevens.

Meanwhile, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers’ campaign is projecting confidence over the surge for the left and Democratic infighting.

"If you think calling to defund the police, abolishing private healthcare for autoworkers, and campaigning with an influencer who said, ‘America deserved 9/11’ are winning messages, I have news for you: Michiganders aren’t buying it,” Alyssa Brouillet, Rogers’ communications director, said in an emailed statement to NOTUS, including an apparent reference to Piker.

Miller cast cold water on that GOP logic and said the progressives are focused on overall success.

"What we need to beat Republicans in the general election in 2026 and then again in 2028 are people who are absolutely unapologetically un-bought and very clear in their values,” she said.

entries.title: The Struggle of Being a No-Corporate-PAC-Money Democrat
entries.summary: “I am deciding whether I'm going to committee or a meeting based on whether I have to meet with individual donors,” one House Democrat said.
entries.content:
An increasing number of Democratic candidates are pledging to reject donations from business-linked political action committees in 2026 — a promise House Democrats say is easier said than done.

“I am deciding whether I'm going to committee or a meeting based on whether I have to meet with individual donors,” one House Democrat, granted anonymity to speak candidly, told NOTUS. “That's fucked up.”

Democrats who take funds from corporate super PACs “perform significantly worse” against a Republican candidate compared to Democrats who reject outside PAC money, according to a recent analysis from the progressive think tank Data for Progress. That leaves candidates facing what is likely to be the most expensive midterm election in history with few good options: take money from corporations and alienate the base, or spend all day, every day, dialing individual donors for dollars.

But the time constraints attached to calling and meeting individual donors can cut into lawmakers’ legislative responsibilities. Members who spoke to NOTUS say they or their campaign teams spend around 10 to 20 hours a week doing what’s known as “call time.”

“That call thing, calling a stranger in California or New York — it kind of sometimes feels a little demoralizing, right?” Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Illinois) told NOTUS.

“It’s less community events sometimes, right? Because the truth is that AIPAC, AI, and crypto want nothing more than someone like me to not be here, so if I don’t have enough money in the bank, they will primary me and it’s really hard to beat $30 million,” continued Ramirez, who said she also spends less time with family because of call time. “There are sacrifices.”

Rep. Dave Min (D-California), who said he spends 20 hours a week fundraising, split between weekends and little pockets of time while he’s in Washington, said it’s important that members are “seen as above reproach.”“So yes, do I have to work harder? Yes. Do I have to spend Saturdays often fundraising instead of like, hanging out with my family? Yes. But that's a decision I made,” Min added.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) told NOTUS that there are “racial and gender dynamics” that come into play in relation to fundraising.

“Women and people of color and people who come from different socioeconomic backgrounds don't always come with the personal network of people who have thousands of dollars to give,” she said.

Corporate cash has ended in the hands of Democrats, including some who have sworn it off, as NOTUS recently reported. And the difficulties attached to rejecting business-linked money has made it so that some members start accepting it.

Rep. Emily Randall (D-Washington) did not take corporate PAC money during her six years in the Washington State Legislature or during her initial bid for Congress. Now, as a freshman House lawmaker, she does.

Randall pivoted to accepting cash from corporations immediately after winning her election in 2024. She recalled how she often had to prioritize making calls over knocking on doors when she was a first-time congressional candidate who'd sworn off corporate money.

“It was hard,” Randall said. “After the ’24 cycle, I was like, ‘Look, now I'm a safe seat member. My job is to raise as much money as possible to support frontline and Red to Blue members.’ I know what that was like as a member from a tough district in the Legislature, and I want to be a team player that helps make sure that my colleagues can keep their seats and that we can win the seats we have to win.”

The first House Democrat who spoke anonymously concurred. Members who pay dues to the caucus’ campaign arm to help vulnerable Democrats are “constantly getting the messages, ‘You need to give your full dues, you need to give your full dues.’ But it’s really hard to pay for your full dues if you don’t take corporate cash.”

Veteran and more high-profile Democrats don’t face the same issue.

Rep. Jim McGovern of Massachusetts made the leap away from taking corporate money in 2018 after he was sworn in as the top Democrat on the House Rules Committee. Between January 2025 and June of this year, McGovern has amassed more than $750,000 in contributions. In 2018, the last election cycle he accepted corporate PAC money, he raised over $1.1 million.

McGovern, who is often captured giving provocative floor speeches, cited C-SPAN and social media as big drivers for his small-donor contributions, but admitted he has an advantage as a 15-term member with a relatively high profile.

“I guess it's harder for a freshman, you know, when you don't have an established platform. People outside your district, you know, may not know you as well,” he said.

A second House Democrat who spoke anonymously told NOTUS that while now their campaign operation averages around 10 to 15 hours a week, “as a first-time candidate, I was doing like 40 hours a week because you don't know anybody and you just have to try to connect with other people.”

In contrast, Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), a pioneer in the no-corporate-PAC movement, said she spends about two hours a month making fundraising calls, with the bulk of her donations coming from text and email campaigns. But, she added, that’s still a hassle.

"I hate it,” Jayapal told NOTUS. "I don't like it. I don't think I should like asking people to give me money.”

One of the priorities in the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ legislative agenda — especially if Democrats win the majority in November, is to pass legislation to limit super PAC contributions.

“There is still a structural problem,” CPC Chair Greg Casar told NOTUS. The legislation, he continued, is “one of the multiple ways that we can eventually just get big money out of politics.”

Rep. Summer Lee (D-Pennsylvania), who leads the Abolish Super PACs Act and co-leads other campaign finance reform legislation, said “Corporations recognize that this is a gap, a loophole in the system.”

“It does two things: It creates an overreliance on their influence in the first place,” Lee said of corporate money. “It also keeps people out. It keeps working class people out. It keeps women out. It keeps particularly Black women, the folks who are going to have the hardest time fundraising, in the back.”

“It is an imbalance that even now members who accept corporate PACs are starting to recognize,” Lee added.

Democratic lawmakers like Reps. Grace Meng of New York, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Mike Thompson of California, who accept corporate PAC money, are listed as co-sponsors for her bill.

The makeup of the district can also have a direct impact on lawmakers’ fundraising ability.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California), who represents the heart of Silicon Valley, touted the need for public financing “so that we reduce that influence” in elections. But he said he sympathizes with his colleagues who do not represent wealthy districts like he does and have a harder time fundraising.

“I don't come at it with some pretense that I'm sort of morally superior to my colleagues when I have access to a lot more wealthy donors than they do,” he told NOTUS.

For members in House Democratic leadership, this is just part of the job. Rep. Lauren Underwood of Illinois, a recruitment co-chair for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee who does not take corporate money, put it simply: “We always have to make fundraising calls. We always have to go travel and do events. I have to go and literally get the money.”

“We are the stars. We are the talent. We have to go get this money to sustain the campaign,” she told NOTUS.

entries.title: So Long, Luis García Jr. (And Hello to Four New Arms.)
entries.summary: On Sunday, the Nats traded García, their longest-tenured player, to the Yankees for four right-handed pitchers.
entries.content:
If every trade is a peek inside a front office’s collective brain, the Nationals’ latest deal — sending Luis García Jr. to the Yankees for four right-handed pitchers on Sunday — only furthers what we’d already learned about the new group running the team: They view pitching as a real organizational weakness and are willing to trade controllable bats to change that.

And rather than always hunting one or two high-upside prospects in trades, they’re up for swapping established talent for a handful players, which reads as having high confidence in their development process.

In this case, the big haul included Jack Cebert, Ben Grable, Yovanny Cruz and Jake Bird. None of them ranked in the Yankees’ top 10 prospects on Baseball America, which slotted Cebert at No. 11, Grable at No. 19 and Cruz at No. 24. Of the four, Cebert is the only starter, a 24-year-old who’s dominated AA in recent weeks. Grable, also 24 and in AA, has an intriguing fastball that’s generated a lot of in-zone whiffs in the minors. Cruz, a 26-year-old with four big league appearances, can run his four-seamer into the triple digits. Bird, 30, has made 227 relief appearances between the Yankees and Rockies and never finished a season with an ERA better than 4.33. Unlike the others, he is no longer a prospect.

Each has their flaws, of course, which is why they were part of a four-player package for a high-end platoon player. But the head says this is a definite win for the Nats, especially given their need for pitching — and especially given that García, 26, was treading water before this season and then turned into a valuable trading chip. Instead of cutting him loose, Paul Toboni, the club’s first-year president of baseball operations, made him a full-time first baseman who mostly played against righties.

The Yankees, first in the American League wild-card standings, will almost certainly use him in a platoon, too. In 374 plate appearances, García has already set a career high with 23 homers, all but three of them against righties. He also has the best slugging percentage (.560) in the National League. And he’s under team control for another season beyond 2026.

So if you’re a Nationals fan, it may feel a bit more complicated for the heart. Signed out of the Dominican Republic in 2016, García was the team’s longest-tenured player, the last on-field link to the best era in the franchise’s short history. Trading him now, as the team is finally on a jagged upswing, can be both strategically sound and emotionally fraught. For five summers, the team has often traded away its most recognizable players, leaving the city starved for reliable connection points. At some point, in theory, the Nats’ short-term ambitions might outweigh the benefits of selling high on a player like García to improve future rosters. That point just isn’t this week.

The trade deadline is 6 p.m. Monday. For the last couple months, ever since the Nats’ strong start proved more than a statistical oddity, Toboni has been saying that team performance could affect his deadline approach. Or put another way: If the Nationals kept winning, Toboni seemed willing to bend his long view to the present.

At the start of last week, with five games to the deadline, the Nats were 55-53, smack in the middle of the wild-card race. Then they lost five in a row, dropping to 4½ games out of the final wild-card spot with four teams in front of them.

Still, despite a crowded, fragile path to the playoffs, Toboni has seemingly sold and bought at the same time. For the Nationals’ first trade of the deadline season, they sent infielder Curtis Mead to the Red Sox for left-handed pitcher Connelly Early, who is on the injured list but could return this month. With the package for García, both Cruz and Bird could immediately contribute to a bullpen that has blown 27 saves. That doesn’t mean the present was the main focus for either of those deals. It does, however, show the front office is interested in addressing short- and long-term needs this summer (and capable of trying both within the same transaction, results pending).

Bird was optioned to AAA after the deal was completed Sunday, as was right-handed reliever Riley Cornelio. That indicates that Cruz could join the team ahead of a series opener in Philadelphia on Monday night. The Nats will have to fill García’s and Cornelio’s spots, at a minimum, since they could also make more trades. Abimelec Ortiz, acquired in the five-player return for MacKenzie Gore last winter, is the logical replacement for García, a left-handed first baseman with a compelling offensive profile. If the Nats use him just like García, he’ll pair with Andrés Chaparro in a platoon at first. The offense, still ranked first in runs scored by a good margin, will need some new energy after losing two players (García and Mead) with an OPS over .850.

And as for what the Nats could do before the deadline, Foster Griffin, their all-star starting pitcher, has attracted a lot of interest. So has shortstop CJ Abrams, though the chances of him moving are far, far lower than the Nationals flipping Griffin for future parts, according to multiple people familiar with the team’s thinking.

The market for starting pitchers has thinned in recent days, with Tarik Skubal (Tigers to Dodgers), Luis Castillo (Mariners to White Sox), Freddy Peralta (Mets to Rays) and Kevin Gausman (Blue Jays to Cubs) all off the board. Broadly, those deals have favored the buyers, though a scarcity of front-line arms could now work in the Nationals’ favor. Then D.C. will make a full assessment of Toboni’s first deadline after 6 p.m.

entries.title: Blanche Cuts a Deal With Cornyn to Get His Nomination Back on Track
entries.summary: The agreement came together despite apparent opposition from Trump, who has vocally expressed support for the $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund.
entries.content:
Sen. John Cornyn has struck a deal with acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and the Justice Department on an in-writing order nixing the “anti-weaponization fund” and limiting the scope of the audit immunity deal struck with President Donald Trump, putting Blanche a step closer to being confirmed as attorney general.

Late on Sunday, Cornyn and Blanche announced the agreement, which featured a formal order that the Texas senator and Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) had been seeking for weeks in order to advance his nomination.

“Sen. Cornyn has reached an agreement with the Department of Justice,” Natalie Yezbick, a Cornyn spokeswoman, said in a statement. “[The DOJ] will be issuing a formal order permanently terminating the anti-weaponization fund and making clear in a binding written document that the scope of the audit settlement is limited to only the plaintiffs, including the President, and the IRS.”

The decision comes ahead of Tuesday’s planned Senate Judiciary Committee markup, which Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Republican leaders scheduled over the weekend in the hopes that a deal would be struck.

A single “no” vote from Cornyn or Tillis would have sunk Blanche’s nomination.

The agreement came together despite apparent opposition from Trump, who has vocally expressed support for the $1.8 billion fund. The president late last week indicated that he was willing to temporarily withdraw Blanche’s nomination until early next year when Cornyn and Tillis, who both lost primaries this year, are set to leave office.

Trump wrote on Truth Social Saturday that he was prepared to “push hard” for the fund to be codified into law despite the reservations of numerous Senate Republicans beyond Cornyn and Tillis.

Blanche posted the pair of orders on his X feed.

“My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions,” Blanche posted shortly before Cornyn publicly agreed to the deal. “We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result issue the following order and update with regard to the May IRS settlement. The Department always welcomes and appreciates productive engagement with all members of Congress.”

entries.title: A Big, Beautiful Parking Garage
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Dulles’ new parking deck, Trump’s golden horses and fans at Commanders training camp.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

THE LATEST

One of the D.C. area’s biggest attractions may soon be a parking garage.

As part of his sweeping $22.5 billion overhaul of Dulles International Airport, President Donald Trump says a new parking deck will be built in front of the historic main terminal with enough space for 32,000 cars.

“It’ll be the largest garage in the world,” he said last week. “It will be beautiful.”

What’s unclear is whether Dulles even needs that much parking. NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle reports that a 2025 master plan for the airport drawn up by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority, which manages Dulles, found that the existing 22,000 parking spots would suffice until at least 2045.

But just to be on the safe side, the authority had drawn up plans for a new parking deck — with one-fifth the capacity of what Trump is pledging.

There are also unanswered questions about the sheer physical scale of Trump’s garage. As proposed, it could stand some 15 stories tall, towering over the iconic terminal designed by Finnish architect Eero Saarinen.

With a garage that big, there’s likely to be “all kinds of issues with throughput of vehicles, wayfinding, ventilation and fire safety,” said local parking expert Bill Boyle. “There’s no precedent for building a parking deck this big.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

GoldHorses_Grid.jpg (16235x7927, AR: 2.05)
Trump’s golden horses have (finally) arrived. In May, NOTUS’ Anna Kramer reported that the National Park Service was re-gilding the four massive horse statues near the Lincoln Memorial with an unusually thick layer of 23.75-karat gold, to the tune of 5 million taxpayer dollars.

The Park Service wanted the horses (known as the Arts of War and Arts of Peace) finished in time for the July Fourth festivities, calling it an “immovable deadline” in their justification for handing out a rushed, no-bid contract this spring. But the rush was for naught: Two of the horses were just unveiled last week, and two more are still covered up. The city’s July Fourth crowds got nothing more than some scaffolding and drapes.

A high-level aide to D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser is parting ways with the city, marking the first big departure in the waning months of the mayor’s time in office. Lindsey Parker, who joined Bowser’s administration more than a decade ago and rose to chief of staff, will next take the reins of the Maryland Stadium Authority. It’s a logical move: Parker’s last role in D.C. government was as senior adviser for the Commanders stadium project.

A Republican senator wants more patriotism in D.C. schools. Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Florida) has introduced a bill that would require that the U.S. flag be displayed in every classroom in D.C. schools, and mandate that students recite the Pledge of Allegiance at the start of every day. (Parents would be allowed to opt their children out.) Moody said the bill would help “restore pride in our nation” and fight an “outrageous curriculum” that includes lessons on LGBTQ+ history. Critics say this is another unnecessary intrusion into the city’s affairs.

Organizers of the popular Cherry Blossom 10-Miler recently warned runners that, starting next year, the race’s “most memorable sections” could be affected or even eliminated by Trump’s planned construction in Memorial Circle and around East Potomac Park.

Preservationists are mounting their latest campaign to stop a Trump-led remake of a D.C. building, seeking an injunction to stop the administration from painting the Eisenhower Executive Office Building white, NBC4 reports.





TRIVIA


In which jurisdiction can you get married without an officiant?

  1. D.C.
  2. Maryland
  3. Virginia
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout-out. The answer will be at the end of tomorrow’s newsletter.





SPORTS

Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson was in Ashburn on Saturday for the first of 11 Commanders practices open to fans. Thousands showed up, with some arriving hours ahead of the 8:30 a.m. start time.

The session featured a lot of fan service, including a fun segment where the offensive linemen ran pass routes. But the biggest reaction of the day came during the appearances of Hall of Famers Darrell Green and John Riggins, who will have new roles with the franchise this season.

The WNBA trade deadline has come and gone, with the Mystics standing pat. Washington will be leaning on the second-youngest roster in league history as it makes a playoff push.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals at Phillies, 6:40 p.m. (MLB.TV)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photos by Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS.

entries.title: Two Senators Are Convinced Trump’s IRS Deal Is Dead. Others, Not So Much.
entries.summary: Todd Blanche’s late-night documents eased political concerns, but not legal questions, on the anti-weaponization fund and immunity deal.
entries.content:
Two Republican holdouts on Todd Blanche’s attorney general nomination said they got the written assurance they needed that President Donald Trump’s $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund is dead.

But the two pages of text on Justice Department letterhead appear to carry little legal weight, according to legal experts.

The documents released late Sunday by Blanche, the acting attorney general, leave ample room for the Trump administration to use other avenues to compensate the president’s allies who claim they were unfairly targeted by federal authorities.

They also keep largely intact a tax-audit immunity deal for Trump and his family, which, along with the fund, was created to settle a lawsuit Trump brought against the IRS over their leaked tax returns.

Blanche’s order is not signed by Trump or other parties in that underlying litigation, raising doubt about its enforceability, according to experts. And because it’s a Justice Department document, not a court filing, Blanche could undo it with the stroke of a pen if he gets the permanent job.

All told, said Rupa Bhattacharyya, a former Justice Department attorney who managed victim compensation funds for the department, the order “feels like a very political move to get the nomination advanced.”

“It’s not clear to me what authority or legal effect the acting attorney general has to modify the settlement agreement on his own behalf,” Bhattacharyya said. “And there’s nothing that stops him from getting confirmed and then rescinding the order that rescinded the order.”

Lawyers in a federal lawsuit challenging the fund were not convinced, either. In a letter Monday to the Justice Department, they called on officials to back up Blanche’s assertions in court. They asked the government to tell them by 5 p.m. whether the Justice Department will file a written declaration saying under penalty of perjury that the fund would not proceed.

“The Trump-Vance administration cannot ask the public or our clients to accept a late-night social media post in place of legally binding action,” said Skye Perryman, who heads Democracy Forward, the legal advocacy group representing the plaintiffs.

Even a Trump ally and prominent backer of the anti-weaponization fund, Mike Howell of the conservative Oversight Project, acknowledged on social media how easily Blanche could reverse his order.

“Can be undone after Tuesday,” Howell wrote over Blanche’s post of the document. “The Anti-Weaponization Fund is great.”

Blanche published the order in an 11 p.m. social media post, calling it the product of “good faith discussions” with lawmakers who were concerned about the settlement in Trump’s IRS lawsuit.

Some lawmakers had objected to the possibility that the anti-weaponization fund could be used to pay rioters from the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. And they also questioned whether the immunity deal could apply to future tax issues or benefit Trump associates not named in the case.

Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, both on the Senate Judiciary Committee, threatened to block Blanche’s nomination without written assurance that the fund had been terminated and the deal modified.

In statements Monday, the senators said they were “pleased” with what they called the “binding” order from Blanche. They are expected to vote along with other Republicans to advance his nomination out of the Judiciary Committee on Tuesday morning.

The order says a May 18 directive from Blanche establishing the fund “is rescinded and shall have no force or effect.”

“No Members were appointed; no funds were transferred; no process for receiving claims was established; no claims were paid,” the document states. “This order establishes, beyond any doubt, that there is no Fund.”

The order also purports to limit Trump’s immunity deal, saying that it “applies by its terms only retroactively,” meaning it would not extend to people outside the lawsuit nor protect the president, his sons or their business from possible future audits.

Legal experts and several Democratic lawmakers said the immunity agreement may have still wiped out tens of millions of dollars or more in potential tax liabilities from Trump and his family.

“Lipstick on this rancid grift is no excuse to confirm him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut) said of Blanche.

Experts also noted that the Justice Department could still pay out claims to Jan. 6 defendants and others alleging political prosecution under the Federal Tort Claims Act.

“If what the senators are concerned about is that payments are going to be made to Jan. 6 defendants, the fact is, a very large number of them have filed claims under the Federal Tort Claims Act. And the Justice Department could be paying out those claims,” said Bhattacharyya, who is legal director at the Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection at Georgetown Law. “The administration never needed the anti-weaponization fund to settle these claims.”

Just last week, the Justice Department agreed to pay a seven-figure settlement to an anti-abortion activist, Paul Vaughn, who was convicted during the Biden administration of blocking access to an abortion clinic. Trump pardoned Vaughn while his case was on appeal.

Speaking with reporters Monday, Trump defended the tax deal and anti-weaponization fund, claiming he and others were wrongfully investigated and prosecuted by previous presidential administrations.

"I view that fund as a positive, and a lot of Republicans do too," Trump said. "I think Todd Blanche agreed to reconfirm things that he's already said, and what he said was OK."

A Justice Department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Barbara McQuade, a former longtime federal prosecutor, said Vaughn’s settlement “shows that they’re not done giving payouts to Trump supporters who claimed to have been the victims of weaponization.”

“They’re just going to do it individually instead of through the settlement fund,” she said. “As a result, this representation by Blanche isn’t worth the paper it’s written on.”

entries.title: Author of Democrats’ 2024 Autopsy Releases ‘Missing’ Chapter
entries.summary: The DNC contends that it never received the document in question.
entries.content:
The author of the Democratic National Committee’s widely panned 2024 postelection autopsy report released what he said is an unpublished chapter on Monday, breathing new life into a scandal that threatens to distract the party as it prepares for the closing stretch of the 2026 midterms.

Paul Rivera, a longtime Democratic consultant, shared the 28-page installment with The New York Times, claiming that the missing document includes questions about President Joe Biden’s decision to run for reelection and addresses frustration that high-earning Democratic elites “drive too much of the decision-making within the ecosystem.”

The consequences of Biden’s decision to run again were not discussed at length in the original 192-page document released in May. In the newly released chapter, Rivera addresses the former president’s decision.

“Is there a single point of failure for 2024? Perhaps it is a decision of the President to seek re-election instead of passing the torch, but Democrats do not have a time machine to go back and change his decision,” Rivera wrote.

Rivera told the Times he personally delivered the chapter in a binder to Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin in January. But Martin and other representatives for the DNC disputed that they had ever seen the chapter in question, and that the “missing” chapter could not be located in an extensive search of the committee’s files.

“That is false,” Martin wrote in a statement. “The only binder I was working with Paul on was for lessons learned materials. This alleged report section was not in any binder I reviewed.”

If the DNC had received the chapter in question from Rivera, it “would have released it with the rest of the report,” Martin said.

Neither NOTUS nor The New York Times could independently verify either account.

The chapter also reviewed Democrats’ declining support from Hispanic, Black, Asian American and Native American voters, and noted that digital consultants had missed the mark with voters.

“They missed important signals about why people were frustrated with Democrats, who seemed not to appreciate or understand their situation,” Rivera wrote — though he did not identify anyone by name.

Martin said “one of [his] key priorities remains, to hold the consultant-industrial complex accountable,” and added that the DNC would have “absolutely” published any “report materials that went after self-enriching consultants,” if the committee had them.

“Whether that was a conscious decision on their part to bury the section for the purposes of hiding a paragraph, I don’t know,” Rivera told The New York Times. “That’s a them question. What I can tell you is they had it, and they made a decision not to release it.”

After submitting files to the DNC in late 2025, Martin allegedly told Rivera he was disappointed with the quality of his work, and the pair met for a discussion in January. Rivera then compiled a new 173-page report that he claims included the chapter in question.

But Martin said his “work with Paul in January is being misrepresented,” because they only discussed documents that outlined “lessons learned.”

“That effort did not include reviewing new report material, only the material the DNC had already received, which is what we released in May,” Martin said.

The original report drew a rebuke by Democrats for its failure to address Biden’s impact on the race and Kamala Harris’ subsequent campaign without an official primary process. The report was also missing an executive summary, even though there was an apparent place for one in the first few pages of the report, with an annotation that the section was not provided by the author.

The entire report included an annotation in red at the top of every page, saying “this document reflects the views of the author, not the DNC.” The committee added in the disclaimer that Rivera did not provide “underlying sourcing, interviews, or supporting data for many of the assertions” contained in the report.

Some Democrats thought the original report failed to draw any meaningful conclusions about where the party went wrong in 2024.

Rivera sought to address the criticism by releasing a 500-page independent autopsy report on Aug. 3, called Blue by 2032, that opens with an accounting of the events surrounding the original report.

“In late December, 2025 the DNC decided to announce it was not releasing a report, and did not release an executive summary. In the ensuing six months, the DNC never asked for a meeting to discuss content, or provided markup or questions to the after-action project team,” Rivera wrote.

The timeline appears to conflict with Rivera’s account of his discussions with Martin in January. Blue by 2032 did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

After the Times released Rivera’s missing chapter, some political analysts said the new document suffers from many of the same problems that plagued the publicly released version of the report.

“I think the author of the DNC autopsy is giving himself too much credit,” Nate Silver, a statistician and the founder of FiveThirtyEight.com, wrote on X. “If you actually read the omitted chapter (good of the NYT to include it), it consists largely of boilerplate and clichés and mentions Biden's decision to run only in passing.”

Neither the original report nor Rivera’s additional chapter make any mention of Israel or its war in Gaza, a crucial issue that split Democratic voters in the lead-up to the 2024 election and continues to be a controversial topic for candidates.

Critics of the original report released by the DNC also took issue with the omission of the conflict, but in a statement at the time Martin acknowledged that a number of key issues were left out of the autopsy.

“I am not proud of this product; it does not meet my standards, and it won’t meet your standards,” Martin said in May. “I don’t endorse what’s in this report, or what’s left out of it.”

entries.title: Golf the Blues Away
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for August 3, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

President Donald Trump complained this morning about the “unbelievably duplicitous” Iranian regime after it denied his assertion that another round of ceasefire negotiations were set to begin.

But he’s having a better time on the links. Trump, 80, apparently won the club championship at his Bedminster golf club in New Jersey over the weekend. He posted video this morning of what he called “the winning shot,” a short chip that landed within a few feet of the hole.

  • “It’s called TALENT, and I have it, and they don’t!” Trump wrote.
The House Ethics Committee recommended Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-North Carolina) for censure over what it classified as inappropriate relationships with staffers.

  • This is the first time the committee has resorted to censure since it knocked former Rep. Charles Rangel (D-New York) in 2010 over improper fundraising, financial disclosures and failure to pay taxes.




THE HILL

Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) have agreed to back Trump’s attorney general nominee, Todd Blanche, after he officially agreed in writing to kill the “anti-weaponization” fund and limit a legal settlement shielding the president and his businesses from IRS audits.

The Senate version of a continuing resolution released over the weekend would prohibit the Office of Management and Budget from implementing an overhaul of the federal grant-approval process that would have handed more power over to the White House.

  • The upper chamber is scheduled to vote this evening on the short-term government funding bill.




THE ADMINISTRATION

The president is weighing whether to fire Jeanine Pirro over her decision to drop charges against a formern Olympian who had been accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, CNN reported.

  • “Frankly, I think she choked, because the judge was really vicious,” Trump told reporters this afternoon.
  • When asked whether he was reconsidering Pirro’s role, Trump called the reporter “fake news.” 
Embattled FIFA boss Gianni Infantino called up Marco Rubio this morning in an attempt to shore up U.S. support and protect his job. He’s facing pressure to resign after abandoning a scheme to sell off shares of the World Cup to Joshua Kushner’s private equity firm, the New York Post reported.

The U.S. dollar is weakening against the Japanese yen today after the U.S. Treasury Department made a rare intervention to prop up the floundering currency last week.

The National Park Service assessed that Trump’s massive arch would “adversely” affect dozens of iconic D.C. monuments.





THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL

The author of the DNC’s 2024 election “autopsy” claimsrevealed that the document made public by embattled chair Ken Martin earlier this year had a missing chapter. It focused on both President Joe Biden’s ill-fated decision to run for reelection and the reasons Democratic operatives did not properly weigh voters’ affordability concerns, according to The New York Times.

  • “That is false,” Martin told the Times. “This alleged report section was not in any binder I reviewed … If we had this in May, we would have released it with the rest of the report.”
