entries.title: Ethics Committee Recommends Censure for Rep. Chuck Edwards Over ‘Inappropriate Conduct’
entries.summary: Edwards denies that the conduct was “intended as a sexual or romantic advance.”
entries.content:
The House Ethics Committee recommended censuring Rep. Chuck Edwards on Monday, citing his alleged inappropriate relationships with staffers.

“The Committee concluded there was substantial reason to believe Representative Edwards violated House Rules related to sexual harassment and hostile workplaces,” the committee wrote in a press release about the North Carolina Republican.

The committee’s report found that Edwards “engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.” Edwards, 65, who has been married since 1980,has denied that the alleged conduct “was intended as a sexual or romantic advance.”

Sources told NOTUS in May that the House Ethics Committee had launched an investigation into allegations that Edwards had an affair with a former staffer who left the office earlier this year. The staffer was Edwards’ former deputy chief of staff, and she was initially hired as a legislative assistant to Edwards when he was a state senator in 2021.

The committee issued a public request in April for anyone to report information about House members or staffers engaging in sexual misconduct.

“Shortly after that announcement, the Committee was informed of allegations regarding Representative Edwards’ conduct towards women in his office and began confidentially reviewing the allegations,” the committee wrote in its 25-page report.

Edwards was aware that his conduct toward the staffers had generated discussion and “rumors” in his office, according to the report.

“Representative Edwards also went beyond norms of professional behavior by giving both women lavish gifts,” the committee wrote. “Both women received numerous gifts from Representative Edwards, including jewelry totaling over $1,000, designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners.”

One of the staffers said she felt “obligated to wear” a necklace Edwards gave her, and the congressman told her he was disappointed when she did not wear it.

The report catalogues instances of alleged inappropriate conduct with the staffers, including the congressman paying for spa treatments, discussing going to strip clubs in D.C. and directing one of the staffers not to notify Edwards’ scheduler about a dinner the pair had planned.

Edwards brought one of the staffers to a holiday event at the White House and told her he wanted the night to be “perfect.” The congressman allegedly pressured the staffer to continue the evening with him and asked her to travel to and from the event in his car with his driver.

Edwards told the committee he did not recall pressuring her that evening, but he acknowledged traveling with her to her home in Virginia because he “felt uncomfortable dumping a young lady on the street.”

The congressman skipped House votes to decorate a Christmas tree with one of the staffers, according to the committee. He also went to that same staffer’s house to “perform chores like yardwork, pick her up and drop her off for events and activities with his driver.”

The committee found that Edwards wrote poems for one of the staffers, “including one that he read at her going away party in the congressional office accompanied by a slideshow, during which he cried.” Multiple staffers testified to the committee that the incident made them feel uncomfortable, and Edwards said he recognized the discomfort among his staff. 

A censure serves as a public condemnation of a congress member’s behavior. The committee will bring Edwards’ censure recommendation for a vote by the full House.

This is the first time the Ethics Committee has recommended censure since it took action against former Rep. Charles Rangel (D-New York) in 2010 over improper fundraising, financial disclosures and failing to pay taxes.

This story has been updated with more details from the Ethics Committee report.

entries.title: States Warn Supreme Court That Trump’s Mail-In Voting Order Would Create Chaos
entries.summary: The Supreme Court will soon decide whether the Trump administration can move forward with the president’s changes ahead of the midterms.
entries.content:
A group of states told the Supreme Court on Monday there would be “extraordinary consequences” if the Trump administration is allowed to move forward with an overhaul of mail-in voting rules so close to the midterm election.

The filing responded to a Trump administration request that the justices allow federal agencies to implement two parts of an executive order that directed the U.S. Postal Service to create mail ballot rules and the Department of Homeland Security to compile a national database of eligible voters.

A lower court order has blocked those parts of the order in nearly half of all states and the District of Columbia.

Those states told the Supreme Court there would be a limited window to correct errors, which could disenfranchise the voters that rely on mail-in voting, such as older Americans and people with disabilities. Other voters would be confused about getting their ballots or whether the USPS would deliver them.

“State and local elections administrators would be forced to divert time and resources away from critical election-preparation tasks,” the states said.

Attorneys for the administration have argued that an injunction against the policies is “premature” because the agencies have not yet implemented the executive order. The states argued that it would “not be sensible” to force states to wait to sue to stop the policies they call “plainly unlawful.”

“It would be extremely difficult — if not impossible — to obtain a definitive judicial resolution with enough time remaining for States to redesign and reorder their ballot mail, train elections officials, and adequately educate the public before the November midterms,” the filing states.

The ongoing court battle stems from a March executive order that would require the Social Security Administration and DHS to create a list of eligible voters for the Postal Service to send ballots to.

The Trump administration is seeking to lift an injunction in a Massachusetts lawsuit, which was brought by 23 states and D.C. In another case brought by Democrats in D.C, an appeals court determined that the legal challenge was premature. The decision upheld a prior D.C. ruling from District Judge Carl Nichols, a Trump appointee, who also said the policies need to be implemented before they can be blocked.

Democrats argued in Monday’s response to the Supreme Court that although the courts consider their arguments to be “unripe,” the administration has clear plans and dates to implement these changes as soon as possible under the looming deadline of Nov. 3.

And the USPS is already moving forward with rulemaking. The Federal Register shows that the agency submitted a rule with changes that comply with the president’s executive order, on the contingency that it succeeds in the courts.

“The proposal to amend the [Domestic Mail Manual] is the subject of active litigation, including two injunctions that are currently being appealed. The Postal Service will not publish a final rule unless and until the government obtains relief from all relevant injunctions,” the rule says.

With the midterms now 92 days away, President Donald Trump continues to push last-ditch efforts to oversee elections and message to voters that noncitizen voting is rampant, despite reports that it occurs rarely.

Several issues would need to be reconciled if the Supreme Court allows the administration to change mail-in voting rules, including how the USPS would screen eligible voters under such a tight deadline. The USPS is already hearing complaints from election officials about delays for mail-in ballots.

entries.title: Trump Says Jeanine Pirro ‘Choked’ in Dropping Reflecting Pool Prosecution
entries.summary: The U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia was seen at the White House after Trump criticized her decision to dismiss the case.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump railed against U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro on Monday, days after her office dropped charges against a man accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and admitted in court the issues were due to “flawed installation by the contractor,” not vandals.

“Jeanine Pirro made a mistake,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday. “There was vandalism.”

The Justice Department moved to dismiss the criminal case on Friday against David Hearn of Maryland, a former Olympian who was indicted by a grand jury on charges of purposefully destroying part of the new coating applied to the pool during a Trump-directed renovation.

The president is weighing firing Pirro after he was “blindsided” by her decision to dismiss Hearn’s case, CNN reported. Pirro was spotted entering the White House’s West Wing on Monday afternoon.

Trump earlier Monday reiterated his assertion that the administration has recordings of vandals cutting the Reflecting Pool with box knives.

“Now I'm not saying I was 100% thrilled with the contractor, but the contractor was rushing,” Trump said. “We wanted to get it open for July 4, and we got it done. But in addition, there was vandalism.”

The president said Pirro visited the Reflecting Pool after the Fourth of July celebration when the water was filled with debris from the record-breaking fireworks display.

Trump said Pirro “choked” after a judge questioned the government’s evidence and the handling of the prosecution. Trump called the judge "vicious” but blamed Pirro for dropping the proceedings against Hearn.

“She folded like an umbrella, and people get away with things,” Trump said. “It's a disgrace.”

Pirro’s filing to dismiss the case cast blame on the Interior Department, saying new information provided to her office undermined the evidence — supplied by Interior and U.S. Park Police — that the damage was “entirely caused by vandals” rather than botched construction.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum backed Trump’s assertion that vandals damaged the Reflecting Pool and touted his commitment to seeing through cases against any alleged vandals.

“We won't back down to deranged people who want to destroy, deface, or degrade our monuments,” Burgum wrote Saturday on X.

Trump and Pirro spoke on the phone on Saturday about the court filing, and one unnamed source told CNN the conversation “wasn’t pretty.”

Hearn, a former Olympic canoeist, was one of at least seven people arrested at the Reflecting Pool over allegations of destruction of property and vandalism, according to the White House. Hearn was arrested June 19 and indicted by a grand jury July 2, and pleaded not guilty.

Hearn’s legal team told MS NOW that he is weighing “all remedies,” including potential legal action, now that his case has been dismissed.
